subject: science
title: Types of Chemical Reactions & Conservation of Atoms
subtitle: Combination, Decomposition, Single & Double Displacement, Activity Series, and Stoichiometric Balancing
curiosity_hook: When two clear liquids suddenly turn bright yellow or a solid disappears into gas bubbles, where do the atoms actually go?
learning_objectives: Classify chemical reactions by atomic rearrangement: Combination, Decomposition, Single Displacement, Double Displacement (Precipitation & Neutralization), and Combustion.
Balance stoichiometric coefficients to verify the Law of Conservation of Matter (equal atom counts per element on reactant and product sides).
Predict whether a single displacement reaction is feasible using the Class 10 Activity Series and halogen reactivity order.

concept_outline.heading: Bond Breaking, Bond Making & Conservation of Matter
concept_outline.summary: In any chemical reaction, reactant bonds break (absorbing energy) and new product bonds form (releasing energy). Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed — so every chemical equation must balance element by element and denote physical states: (s), (l), (g), (aq).
concept_outline.worked_example: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) conserves 1 C, 4 H, and 4 O atoms across both sides.

concept_outline.heading: Five Rearrangement Classes
concept_outline.summary: Combination (A + B → AB, usually exothermic), Decomposition (AB → A + B via heat/electricity/light, endothermic), Single Displacement (A + BC → AC + B when A is more reactive than B), Double Displacement / Metathesis (AB + CD → AD + CB producing precipitate or water), and Combustion (exothermic oxidation with O₂).
concept_outline.worked_example: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s)↓ + 2KNO₃(aq) swaps Pb²⁺ and K⁺ ions to yield an insoluble yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide.

concept_outline.heading: Reactivity Series & Impossible Displacements
concept_outline.summary: Not every written equation occurs in nature. A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its salt or acid (e.g., Zn displaces H from HCl, and F₂ displaces Cl from NaCl), whereas a less reactive element cannot (Cl₂ cannot displace F from NaF).

key_terms.definition: Two or more elements or compounds combine to form a single product (A + B → AB); typically exothermic.
Breakdown of a single compound into simpler substances by absorbing heat energy (e.g., CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂).
Ordered list of elements from most reactive (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe...) to least reactive (Cu, Ag, Au, Pt) determining single displacement feasibility.
Double displacement reaction between aqueous solutions that produces an insoluble solid compound (precipitate ↓).
Double displacement reaction where an acid reacts with a base to produce salt and water (e.g., NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O).

controls.label: Choose Approved Textbook Reaction (6 Scenarios including 1 Infeasible Test)
controls.description: Switch between Combination, Thermal Decomposition, Single Displacement, Precipitation, Neutralization, and the NaF + Cl₂ activity-series limit.
controls.keyboard_equivalent: Tab to scenario buttons and press Enter or Space.

controls.label: Step 1 — Predict Reaction Classification
controls.description: Make an ungraded prediction before running the virtual bench.
controls.keyboard_equivalent: Select any prediction button via keyboard.

controls.label: Step 2 — Interactive Stoichiometric Coefficient Balancer (+ / −)
controls.description: Adjust integer coefficients (1–4) for each reactant and product and watch live particle-count bars prove conservation of atoms.
controls.keyboard_equivalent: Press Increment/Decrement buttons for each species.

expected_observations: Every feasible balanced reaction produces identical reactant and product atom counts for every chemical element.
Lead(II) nitrate + potassium iodide yields a bright yellow insoluble precipitate (PbI₂).
Sodium fluoride + chlorine produces NO reaction because fluorine is higher in halogen reactivity than chlorine.
limitations: Virtual bench models stoichiometry, particle counts, and qualitative observations under standard textbook conditions; it does not simulate kinetics or hazardous real-world side reactions.
Do not treat virtual experiments as instructions for mixing chemicals outside a teacher-supervised school laboratory.
interaction.safety_note: Conceptual virtual simulation only. Acids, alkalis, halogen gases, and lead salts are hazardous and must never be handled at home.

storyboard.title: Predict Before Mixing
storyboard.learner_action: Choose a reaction (e.g., Zn + HCl) and select its predicted reaction class before executing.
storyboard.expected_response: Prediction is recorded without grading penalty.

storyboard.title: Run Bench & Inspect Particle Conservation
storyboard.learner_action: Run the virtual reaction and inspect the reactant vs product particle representation.
storyboard.expected_response: Observe the qualitative change (gas bubbles / yellow precipitate / no change) and unbalanced atom counts.

storyboard.title: Balance Coefficients & Test the Impossible Reaction
storyboard.learner_action: Adjust stoichiometric coefficients until every element bar turns green (balanced), then test NaF + Cl₂ to verify reactivity-series limits.
storyboard.expected_response: Atom conservation is mathematically confirmed; NaF + Cl₂ explains why no reaction occurs.

steps.heading: Combination: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)
steps.description: Reactants: 2 H, 2 Cl. Products: 2 H, 2 Cl. Two elements form one compound (exothermic).

steps.heading: Thermal Decomposition: CaCO₃(s) —Heat→ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
steps.description: Reactants: 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O. Products: 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O. One compound splits on heating (endothermic).

steps.heading: Single Displacement: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)↑
steps.description: Reactants: 1 Zn, 2 H, 2 Cl. Products: 1 Zn, 2 H, 2 Cl. Zinc is above Hydrogen in the activity series.
steps.key_takeaway: Compare NaF + Cl₂: no reaction because Cl is less reactive than F.

steps.heading: Double Displacement (Precipitation): Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s)↓ + 2KNO₃(aq)
steps.description: Reactants: 1 Pb, 2 N, 6 O, 2 K, 2 I. Products: identical counts. Yellow solid PbI₂ precipitates.
steps.key_takeaway: Cations exchange partners to form an insoluble precipitate.

steps.heading: Double Displacement (Neutralization): NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
steps.description: Reactants: 1 Na, 1 O, 2 H, 1 Cl. Products: identical counts. Acid + Base → Salt + Water.
steps.key_takeaway: Every balanced equation strictly obeys the Law of Conservation of Matter.

question_bank.prompt: Why does the reaction 2NaF(aq) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(aq) + F₂(g) NOT occur spontaneously, whereas 2NaCl(aq) + F₂(g) → 2NaF(aq) + Cl₂(g) does?
question_bank.hint: Check the relative reactivity of Fluorine and Chlorine in the textbook (p. 141).

options.label: Fluorine is more reactive than Chlorine, so Chlorine cannot displace Fluorine from NaF.
options.feedback: Correct! In single displacement reactions, only a more reactive element can displace a less reactive element from its aqueous compound.

options.label: Chlorine has fewer atoms than Fluorine in the equation.
options.feedback: Both sides have 2 Na, 2 F, and 2 Cl atoms — feasibility depends on chemical reactivity, not just balancing symbols on paper.

options.label: Sodium cannot combine with Chlorine in aqueous solution.
options.feedback: NaCl is completely stable in water; the barrier is that Cl₂ cannot replace the more reactive F⁻ ion.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Science p. 141: Fluorine occupies a higher position in Group 17 and is more active than Chlorine, so F₂ displaces Cl⁻ from NaCl, not the reverse.

question_bank.prompt: What stoichiometric coefficients balance the precipitation equation: ___ Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + ___ KI(aq) → ___ PbI₂(s)↓ + ___ KNO₃(aq)?
question_bank.hint: Count the two NO₃ groups on the left and the two I atoms in PbI₂ on the right.

options.feedback: Spot on! 1 Pb, 2 N, 6 O, 2 K, and 2 I atoms appear on both sides.
With 1 KI you only have 1 I atom on the left, which cannot form PbI₂ (2 I atoms) or balance the 2 nitrate groups.
That creates 4 nitrate groups on the left vs 1 on the right and 4 iodine atoms on the right vs 1 on the left.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂↓ + 2KNO₃ balances Pb (1=1), N (2=2), O (6=6), K (2=2), and I (2=2).

question_bank.prompt: Using the Class 10 Activity Series (p. 141), which metal will displace hydrogen gas from dilute hydrochloric acid: Zinc (Zn) or Silver (Ag)?
question_bank.hint: Find where Hydrogen sits in the activity series compared to Zn and Ag.

options.label: Zinc (Zn), because Zinc is placed above Hydrogen in the activity series.
options.feedback: Correct! Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)↑ proceeds because Zn is more reactive than H, whereas Ag sits below H.

options.label: Silver (Ag), because Silver is a precious metal below Hydrogen.
options.feedback: Metals below Hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au, Pt) are less reactive than Hydrogen and do not displace H₂ from dilute HCl.

options.label: Neither Zinc nor Silver can react with hydrochloric acid.
options.feedback: Zinc readily displaces hydrogen from dilute HCl, releasing H₂ gas bubbles.

question_bank.worked_explanation: In the activity series K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Ag > Au > Pt, Zinc lies above Hydrogen while Silver lies below it.

question_bank.prompt: How do combination reactions and thermal decomposition reactions generally differ in terms of heat energy?
question_bank.hint: Compare bond formation in synthesis vs bond breaking in thermolysis (Table 10.1, p. 142).

options.label: Combination reactions generally release energy (exothermic), whereas thermal decomposition absorbs heat (endothermic).
options.feedback: Correct! Forming new bonds in combination reactions releases heat, while breaking bonds in thermal decomposition requires continuous heat input.

options.label: Both always absorb heat and never release energy.
options.feedback: Most combination reactions release energy as new bonds form.

options.label: Decomposition creates new atoms from heat energy.
options.feedback: Heat breaks existing chemical bonds to rearrange atoms; it never creates new atoms.

question_bank.worked_explanation: Table 10.1 (p. 142): Combination joins reactants into a single product releasing energy; decomposition splits a single compound absorbing energy.

worked_feedback: Always check atom conservation element-by-element after adjusting coefficients.
In single displacement reactions, verify feasibility with the activity series before assuming products form.

flashcards.front: What do the physical-state symbols (s), (l), (g), and (aq) mean in a chemical equation?
flashcards.back: (s) = Solid, (l) = Liquid, (g) = Gas, (aq) = Aqueous solution (dissolved in water).

flashcards.front: Name the three classes of decomposition reactions by energy source.
flashcards.back: Thermal decomposition (heat — Thermolysis), Electrolytic decomposition (electricity — Electrolysis), and Photo decomposition (light — Photolysis, e.g., 2AgBr → 2Ag + Br₂).

flashcards.front: Why does whitewashing walls with slaked lime Ca(OH)₂ produce a shiny finish after 2–3 days?
flashcards.back: Slaked lime reacts slowly with atmospheric CO₂ to form a thin layer of solid calcium carbonate (CaCO₃): Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l).

flashcards.front: What visible change occurs when aqueous Pb(NO₃)₂ and KI are mixed?
flashcards.back: A bright yellow insoluble precipitate of Lead(II) iodide (PbI₂↓) forms via double displacement.
